 Wreaths Across America reports low donations for Fort Jackson National Cemetery 
 Organizers say they are thousands of wreaths short of their goal with a December 1 deadline approaching 
 Thousands of veterans buried at Fort Jackson National Cemetery are at risk of not receiving a wreath this holiday season as donations lag behind previous years. By Kaila Paige Published : Oct. 22, 2026 at 3:44 PM EDT | Updated : 3 hours ago Share Add Us On Google Add as a preferred source on Google COLUMBIA, S.C. (WIS) - Thousands of veterans buried at Fort Jackson National Cemetery are at risk of not receiving a wreath this holiday season as donations lag behind previous years.
 Organizers with Wreaths Across America say donations are coming in slower than usual. There are 14,000 gravesites to honor at the cemetery, but organizers have received approximately 3,000 donations so far.
 The program receives no federal funding, leading organizers to express concern that thousands of resting sites could sit empty.
 Shortage threatens 18-year streak 
 Mike Brown, location coordinator for Wreaths Across America at Fort Jackson, said the location has never missed its goal in the past 18 years.
 “Our goal each year is to make sure that every headstone at Fort Jackson National Cemetery has a wreath on it. The final goal should be 14,000 wreaths that need to be laid by December 19, 2026. Currently, we stand at 3,000 wreaths so far,” Brown said.
 “In comparison to other years, we’re lagging behind where we normally would be,” said Mike Brown, location coordinator for Wreaths Across America at Fort Jackson. “While it’s a little abnormal, we’re optimistic that the Midlands community will come through for us and make those donations and help us hit our goal.” 
 What the wreaths represent
 Heather Renee Johnson, logistics and volunteer coordinator, said the wreaths are not decorative holiday items.
 “They are not holiday wreaths. They truly are memorial wreaths. And they are made very intentionally where each of the bows within the wreath represent a different characteristic that it takes to be a veteran,” Johnson said.
 Brown said the organization’s mission extends beyond the wreaths themselves.
 “Our mission as an organization is to remember, honor, and teach. So we’re remembering those that sacrificed. We’re honoring those that gave their lives,” Brown said.
 Johnson said reading each veteran’s name aloud during the ceremony is part of that mission.
 “It’s an honor to hear people read that person’s name out loud so that that veteran is never forgotten,” Johnson said.
 Impact on visiting families 
 Brown said missing wreaths would be noticeable to families who visit the cemetery.
 “When families show up and they just walk the grounds and it’s peaceful and it’s a beautiful tranquil setting and seeing a notion of wreaths laying out. It’s really something that, it’s hard to out into words and I couldn’t imagine being in a situation where families have to come out and notice that entire sections are missing,” Brown said.
 Johnson said a wreath on every headstone sends a message to families.
 “When they walk through here the day after and they see a wreath on every headstone, it’s a reminder that the community came out to support them, to honor them, and to thank them,” Johnson said.
 The deadline to sponsor a wreath is Dec. 1. All remaining wreaths must be ordered and shipped from Maine in time for the ceremony.
 The wreath-laying ceremony will take place on Dec. 19.
